articles.title: Why Your API Is Slow: Understanding and Fixing N+1 Queries
articles.excerpt: When an API endpoint starts responding in seconds rather than milliseconds, our first instinct as backend engineers is often to blame the infrastructure. We think about throwing more CPU cores at the…
articles.body: When an API endpoint starts responding in seconds rather than milliseconds, our first instinct as backend engineers is often to blame the infrastructure. We think about throwing more CPU cores at the server, increasing database connection pools, or scaling out instances. However, server hardware is rarely the real bottleneck. In most cases, an API is slow because it is making 500 database round trips when it only needed to make one. This performance issue is known as the N+1 query problem , and it creeps into almost every application that uses an Object-Relational Mapper (ORM) to handle related database records. What is the N+1 Query Problem? The pattern usually looks innocent in code. Suppose you want to return a list of 50 books along with each book's author.
articles.author: tanmay kuamr chaurasia

articles.title: I got tired of rebuilding preview environments, so I built Stagd
articles.excerpt: Hi dev.to! I'm Sten, a developer in Norway. This is my first post here, so let me start with the thing I've been building. Every few projects, I'd end up building preview environments for pull request…
articles.body: Hi dev.to! I'm Sten, a developer in Norway. This is my first post here, so let me start with the thing I've been building. Every few projects, I'd end up building preview environments for pull requests again: shell scripts, a GitHub Actions workflow, some glue to start a database and post a link. It worked, and then the next project needed it all over again. I kept waiting for a product that made this easy and still let me keep my own compose file, my own compute and my own data. It didn't show up, so I built it. It's called Stagd . The problem it solves Most teams have one staging environment and more changes than it can hold. Someone deploys their branch, someone else overwrites it, and the reviewer opens a link that's running somebody else's code.

articles.title: Proxy-Authorization belongs to the proxy, not the application
articles.excerpt: Proxy-Authorization belongs to the proxy, not the application HTTP has two related authentication headers with different scopes. Authorization identifies the client to the origin resource. Proxy-Autho…
articles.body: Proxy-Authorization belongs to the proxy, not the application HTTP has two related authentication headers with different scopes. Authorization identifies the client to the origin resource. Proxy-Authorization identifies the client to a proxy. The names are close enough that a chain of reverse proxies and application gateways can blur them. RFC 9110 describes Proxy-Authorization as applying to the next inbound proxy that requested authentication. When multiple proxies are present, the first inbound proxy that expects the credentials consumes them. A proxy may relay them to the next proxy if that is how the proxies cooperatively authenticate, but it is not a general requirement to pass them to the origin application. That distinction is the core of the boundary.

articles.title: European-Japanese BepiColombo probe arrives in orbit around Mercury today
articles.excerpt: The BepiColombo spacecraft will finally arrive in orbit around Mercury today (Nov. 21), more than eight years after leaving its home planet.
articles.body: Mercury is about to receive a robotic visitor from Earth. The BepiColombo mission — a joint effort of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency ( JAXA ) — will arrive in orbit around Mercury today (Nov. 21), more than eight years after leaving its home planet. The big moment will come after an orbit-insertion burn, which is scheduled to begin today at 1:24 p.m. EST (1824 GMT) and last for 37 minutes. BepiColombo consists of two main spacecraft: ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO), also known as Mio.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 20, 1998:  Russia launches 1st module of International Space Station as construction begins on the largest human-built structure in orbit
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 20, 1998, the first piece of the International Space Station launched into orbit. It was just one piece, but the foundation of something much larger.
articles.body: On Nov. 20, 1998, the first piece of the International Space Station launched into orbit. The 42,000-pound module is called Zarya, and it's about the size of a tour bus. Zarya launched on board a Russian Proton rocket . Two weeks later, NASA's STS-88 shuttle mission aboard Endeavour brought the Unity module into space. The STS-88 astronauts connected the two modules in orbit. Zarya was built by the Russians, but it was paid for by the United States. NASA contracted a Russian company to build it for half the price of what the American company Lockheed Martin would have charged. These days, Zarya is mainly used for storage and for external fuel tanks. The module also has docking ports for Russian Progress cargo ships and Soyuz spacecraft that carry crews to and from the space station.

articles.excerpt: Researchers are calling for a moratorium on industrial exploitation of the moon, fearing the lunar environment may suffer irreversible damage if things move too fast.
articles.body: Researchers are calling for a moratorium on industrial exploitation of the moon, fearing that rapid development could cause irreversible environmental damage and destroy invaluable scientific material. Both China and the U.S. are pushing forward with plans to establish permanent human settlements on the moon by the end of the next decade. Commercial players want to build businesses supporting these future explorers by mining for resources such as water , construction materials, industrial metals and rare earth minerals. However, some scientists argue that a temporary ban on lunar industrialization is necessary to allow regulations to catch up and limit what can be allowed in order to prevent a moon rush from destroying the pristine lunar environment.
